title: How to Choose the Right Subscription Payment Methods for Each Southeast Asian Market
summary: See how subscription payment methods differ across Southeast Asia, and choose the local mix that converts sign-ups and protects your recurring revenue.
body_text: Choosing which subscription payment methods to offer in Southeast Asia starts with how each country in the region has its own payment preference, and the method most customers use in one market can be a minority option in the next. Recurring billing is usually associated with cards, and in several large markets that association holds. According to the 2026 State of Subscriptions Report , subscription transactions in the United States run mostly on debit cards at 48.8%, followed by credit cards at 34.7% and PayPal at 9.6%. In EMEA, debit cards also lead at 50.9%, ahead of PayPal at 27.7% and credit cards at 12.8%. Southeast Asia calls for a different approach. Payment behavior across the region is fragmented , and customers do not treat cards as the default for digital purchases. Also read: Subscription Payments in Southeast Asia: What Businesses Need to Know A subscription payment method is the instrument a customer authorizes once and your business then charges on a repeating schedule, whether that is a card, an e-wallet, a bank account, or a direct debit arrangement. Because a single authorization has to hold for months or years, the method you offer at sign-up affects whether a customer subscribes at all and whether every renewal after that clears without your team chasing it. What this article covers: What to weigh when selecting payment methods for a recurring model, from customer familiarity to operational scalability How payment behavior differs across Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Singapore Why a card-only setup limits both reach and renewal performance in most of the region What a multi-market subscription payment strategy involves beyond payment method coverage How Xendit supports recurring collection across local payment methods through one integration Before comparing markets, it helps to be clear on what makes a payment method work for a recurring model. What to consider when choosing subscription payment methods Selecting a subscription payment method involves more than picking whichever option ranks highest in a market. The method has to work at three separate moments in the customer relationship, and weakness at any one of them costs revenue: Familiarity at checkout Customers open the same e-wallet or bank app several times a week, so those options need no explanation when they appear at checkout. An unfamiliar payment option asks the customer to stop and consider something new at the exact moment they are deciding whether to commit, and a share of them hesitate and leave instead of working it out. Ease of authorization at sign-up A subscription asks the customer to approve future charges, which takes more trust than a single purchase. Every extra step at that moment adds risk, whether that is registering a new account, retrieving card details they do not have on hand, or completing a verification flow they have not seen before. Each one gives the customer another reason to abandon sign-up before the first payment clears. Reliability at renewal After sign-up, your business charges the customer without them present. Whether that charge goes through depends on whether the method stays funded and active over time. An e-wallet a customer tops up weekly behaves very differently from a card they keep for occasional use, and that difference affects your renewal success rate month after month. Local relevance has become a measurable part of conversion. Mastercard reports that 77% of online purchases worldwide are now completed with local payment methods , which reflects how much more likely customers are to finish a transaction when they see options they already trust. The cost of getting this wrong is higher for a subscription business than for a one-time sale. When a retail customer leaves at checkout, you lose one order. When a subscriber leaves at checkout, you lose every payment they would have made for as long as they stayed subscribed. The second consideration is operational . Supporting a long list of local methods across six markets creates a cost of its own when each method arrives with a separate integration, settlement flow, and reporting format. What works is a single system that handles both sides, giving customers broad local payment coverage at the front end while your team keeps payment tracking, reconciliation, and reporting in one place, with compliance covered in each market where you collect. These criteria only turn into decisions once you know what customers in each market actually use, and the gap between markets is significant. How each Southeast Asian market prefers to pay, and what to offer for subscriptions Worldpay's 2026 Global Payments Report measures overall online payment preference in each market, and those habits shape subscriptions too, since customers commit to recurring payments most easily on the methods they already use day to day. Here is how customers across selected Southeast Asian markets prefer to pay online: Indonesia: E-wallet and bank-based behavior dominates Digital wallets account for 42% of e-commerce payment methods in Indonesia, with account-to-account transfers at 34% . Credit cards account for 5% . A card-led subscription offer would compete for a narrow slice of this market. The practical route for your business is a payment mix built around how Indonesians prefer to pay, using e-wallets, direct debit, virtual accounts, or QR payments, with cards kept available for the segment that prefers them. Malaysia: Bank transfers lead, with cards in a supporting role Malaysia leans toward account-to-account payments at 35% , followed by digital wallets at 26% and credit cards at 16% . Card usage holds up better here than in most of the region while still trailing bank-based payment. The implication for your sign-up flow is a bank-first default with wallet support alongside it. Cards are still worth offering in Malaysia, though they work better as one of several options than as the only way for a customer to subscribe. Thailand: The region's strongest account-to-account market Account-to-account transfers account for 44% of e-commerce payments in Thailand, the highest share of any market in this comparison, while credit cards account for 10% . For a subscription business entering Thailand, recurring collection has to work over bank rails to reach the majority of customers. A card-only setup would miss the way most Thai customers already pay online. Vietnam: Wallet-led, with bank transfers close behind Digital wallets lead in Vietnam at 38% , followed by account-to-account transfers at 28% and credit cards at 12% . Two payment behaviors carry most of the volume here, so your business benefits from supporting both instead of choosing between them. Offering a wallet option and a bank-based option covers the majority of customers at sign-up and gives renewals a second path when the first method fails. Philippines: Strong e-wallet adoption alongside continued cash use Digital wallets account for 41% of e-commerce payments in the Philippines, while cash-based methods still account for 23% and credit cards for 11% . Cash creates a specific complication for recurring models, since a cash payment cannot be charged automatically on a schedule. Converting cash-comfortable customers into subscribers means giving them a digital method they already trust at sign-up, which in this market usually means a digital wallet, then keeping the renewal experience predictable enough for that method to stay in place. Singapore: The regional exception on cards Singapore is the most card-friendly market in this group, with credit cards at 34% . Digital wallets still lead at 40% . Cards can carry a larger share of your subscriber base here than anywhere else in the region. Wallet support remains worth building, both to serve customer preference and to keep your checkout consistent with the markets you expand into next. One theme runs across most of these markets. E-wallets make up a large share of how customers prefer to pay online, leading outright in Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Singapore, and holding a meaningful share even where account-to-account transfers lead. For a subscription business, offering recurring payments through e-wallets and local bank-based methods lets customers pay with what they already use. Also read: Why Southeast Asia Is Becoming a High-Growth Market for Subscription Businesses Why card-only subscription payments limit growth Payment behavior in the six markets above leads to one conclusion for regional planning. In four of them, credit cards hold the smallest share among the main payment categories, and in Singapore, where cards perform best, e-wallets still carry more volume. A card-only subscription setup therefore reaches a minority of potential subscribers across most of Southeast Asia. The cost of that decision shows up in three places: Fewer completed sign-ups Customers who reach checkout without their usual payment option often leave instead of switching methods, so the subscription never starts. Weaker renewal performance A card that a customer keeps for occasional use is more likely to expire, be left unfunded, or be replaced without an update reaching your billing records. Slower revenue compounding Recurring revenue grows through retained subscribers, so every lost sign-up and every failed renewal removes value from all future months, not only the current one. Demand for your product can be real while very little of it reaches your revenue line, simply because customers cannot subscribe or renew on a method they trust. Also read: How to Scale Subscription Payments in Southeast Asia Without Rebuilding Your Payment System How to build a multi-market subscription payment strategy Payment method coverage handles the collection side. Sustained subscription growth across several markets depends on the surrounding model as well, from how clearly you present value to how quickly you recover a failed charge. Six practices make the biggest difference for businesses operating across the region: Start with a clear value proposition Customers need to understand why a subscription is worth paying for repeatedly before they authorize a recurring charge. Whether the offer covers content, software, services, or recurring products, that value should be evident before the commitment. High barriers to entry work against it.When the Financial Times reduced free articles for nonsubscribers from three to zero , website visits fell by roughly 30% and new subscriber numbers declined over the longer term. Letting customers sample the product first gives your pricing page something to build on. Remove friction from sign-up and onboarding Sign-up is where a large share of potential subscribers drop off. A long sign-up process, unclear billing terms, or a missing payment method can end the relationship before the first charge.Practical fixes include keeping sign-up on a single page, minimizing steps, allowing stored details to auto-populate, and accepting the payment methods relevant to the customer's country. That last point matters most in Southeast Asia, where the preferred method changes at each border. Offer flexible billing and payment options Customers differ in how they want to be billed as much as in how they want to pay. Monthly and annual cycles, bundled packages, tiered plans, and multiple local payment methods all widen the group of customers who can say yes.Flexibility after sign-up counts too, since customers expect to change a payment method, pause, or cancel without contacting support. Making cancellation simple costs some short-term revenue and builds the trust that brings customers back later. Reduce failed payments and involuntary churn Involuntary churn happens when a subscription ends because a payment failed, even though the customer still wanted to keep it. It is one of the most recoverable losses in a subscription business. Expired cards are a common trigger, and card account updater tools refresh stored card details automatically when a number or expiry date changes.In markets where most customers pay by e-wallet or bank transfer, the same protection comes from retry logic, payment reminders, and a second payment method saved on the plan that your system can charge when the first one fails. Billing setups that recognize a declined recurring charge immediately and give the customer a short path to fix it recover revenue that would otherwise lapse. Use customer data to improve retention Recurring billing generates a continuous record of engagement, churn, payment success, and renewal behavior. Tracked properly, that record shows which customers need re-engagement, which offers perform best, and where the payment journey breaks down.Reviewing payment success by method and by market deserves particular attention in Southeast Asia, since a method that performs well in one country can underperform in another. Choose a payment partner that can scale across markets Expansion multiplies the work when each new country requires its own integration, billing flow, and reconciliation process. A partner covering local payment methods, recurring billing, reporting, and reconciliation across markets lets you localize the customer experience while backend operations stay in one place. The evaluation for the right payment partner should include whether the provider can service recurring payments across the markets and currencies you plan to reach, and whether adding a new market becomes a configuration change or a new engineering project . These six practices work as a set, and each one gets harder to hold in place with every market you add, since every country brings its own payment methods, billing flows, and reconciliation work. Removing that repeat build is what a regional payment partner should take off your team. Also read: Recurring Billing at Enterprise Scale: How to Automate Subscription Payments in Southeast Asia How Xendit helps your business support subscription payments and beyond The requirements above describe what a subscription business in Southeast Asia needs from its payment layer. Closing that gap for businesses collecting across the region is what our payment infrastructure is built for. What Xendit offers Recurring payments across the methods each market prefers Xendit lets your business accept subscription payments across multiple methods , including e-wallets, direct debit, cards, and other local channels, so recurring collection reaches customers well beyond the card-holding segment, which is where most of the addressable base in this region falls. Recurring billing you can configure around your model Xendit supports customized schedulers, billing cycles, retry settings, customer notifications, and flexible payment options. Together these reduce manual collection work and improve payment success from sign-up through to renewal. One platform for regional payment method coverage You can activate the payment channels each market prefers without commissioning a separate build for every country, which keeps your local mix flexible as your payment data comes in. Licensing that holds up in procurement review Xendit holds regulatory licenses across its operating markets, which supports the compliance assessment most enterprise teams run before payment acceptance, recurring billing, settlement, and customer payment flows go live. Room for the payment flows that come after subscriptions Many businesses start with recurring payments and later add one-time payments, invoices, or hosted checkout as the model expands. Xendit handles these payment types alongside its full range of payment methods through one platform , so transactions stay visible in one place and entering a new market avoids standing up a separate system. Build a subscription payment mix that fits each Southeast Asian market Southeast Asia rewards subscription businesses that collect the way local customers prefer to pay. Market data gives you the starting point for that decision, and the payment infrastructure behind it determines how much of the demand becomes recurring revenue you can count on. Ready to match your subscription payments to each market you serve? Create your Xendit account or talk to our team and start collecting subscription payments with the right payment methods for your customers. FAQ for subscription businesses in Southeast Asia: Choosing payment methods What is the best payment method for subscription businesses in Southeast Asia? There is no single best method for the whole region because preference changes by country. E-wallets and bank transfers lead in Indonesia, Vietnam, and the Philippines, account-to-account payments lead in Thailand and Malaysia, and cards perform strongest in Singapore alongside e-wallets. Xendit lets your business collect recurring payments across the payment methods each market prefers, including e-wallets, direct debit, and cards through one integration, so the mix can differ by market without a separate setup for each. How do automatic subscription payments work with e-wallets and bank transfers? Yes. The customer authorizes the arrangement once at sign-up, and later charges collect automatically on the schedule you set, in the same way a card mandate works. Xendit supports recurring collection across the payment methods customers in each market already use, such as e-wallets, direct debit, and cards, which is what allows subscription billing to function in markets where card penetration stays low. How does cash usage in markets like the Philippines affect subscription billing? Cash cannot be charged automatically, so customers who usually pay in cash need to move to a digital method at sign-up, most often a wallet. The practical approach is offering the digital wallet they prefer to use and keeping renewals predictable enough for that method to remain in place. Xendit's local payment method coverage gives customers in these markets a familiar option at sign-up, which is what makes a recurring relationship possible in the first place. Can a subscriber keep a backup payment method on the same plan? Yes, and it protects revenue in markets where wallet balances and card details change often. Linking more than one method to a plan means a renewal can still clear when the primary method fails. Xendit allows multiple payment methods on a single subscription plan , alongside retry settings and customer notifications that recover charges after a failed attempt. Which payment methods should you launch first when entering a new Southeast Asian market? Start with the methods that carry the largest share of payments in that market, which across most of Southeast Asia means e-wallets and account-to-account transfers, then confirm which of them support recurring authorization and set a launch timeline your finance team can work with. Launching with the top one or two methods usually covers the majority of customers, with further additions guided by your own payment success data. With Xendit , extra channels activate within the same integration , so a market can launch quickly and widen its method mix later.

title: How does a solar panel work? A simple guide
summary: How does a photovoltaic solar panel work? PV effect, cells, inverter, self-consumption: everything explained with SunPower.
body_text: You see the sun shining on your roof and wonder how to turn that solar radiation into free electricity for your home ? Good news: the way a photovoltaic solar panel works is much simpler than it seems. This guide explains everything step by step, without unnecessary jargon. Solar energy: an infinite resource within reach of your roof Our sun is a natural nuclear power plant. Every hour, it sends enough energy to Earth to cover global needs for an entire year . And yet, we only capture a tiny fraction of it. The good news? Europe is well positioned to take advantage of it. By 2025, the EU’S photovoltaic fleet reached around 406 GW of installed capacity . In June that year, solar energy was even the main source of energy produced in the EU at 22%. Solar electricity production is growing rapidly – in 2025 it increased by more than 20% compared to 2024, for the 4th consecutive year. With rising and volatile energy prices , switching to solar has never been more relevant. You might be thinking: Solar energy does not produce electricity continuously. And that’s true - it generates mainly during the day, when sunlight is strongest, which also happens to be when electricity demand is highest. With a solar battery, however, you can store this energy for use at night. Solar plus energy storage is becoming a winning combination. How does a photovoltaic solar panel work, step by step? A solar panel works thanks to a fascinating physical phenomenon: the photovoltaic effect . Here’s how this system converts sunlight into usable electricity. Residential solar panels capture sunlight on the roof, where the photovoltaic effect begins generating clean electricity. Step 1: Solar radiation hits the photovoltaic cells The sun emits energy particles called photons . These photons travel 149.6 million kilometers in just 8.5 minutes before reaching your roof. When they hit the photovoltaic cells of a solar panel, they release electrons from their atoms. This is how an electric current is created. Step 2: The photovoltaic effect produces electricity Each photovoltaic cell is made of silicon , the same material used in semiconductors in your electronic devices. Each cell is built with a positive layer and a negative layer. Together, they create an electric field that sets electrons in motion. When electrons circulate in this field, they generate electricity: this is the photovoltaic effect in action. Several photovoltaic cells assembled together form a solar panel . Several panels together form a complete photovoltaic system . The more panels you install, the more solar energy and electricity you produce for your home. Step 3: The inverter converts direct current into alternating current Solar panels produce direct current (DC) : electrons flow in a single direction. However, your home operates on alternating current (AC) — the type supplied by the power grid. The conversion is handled by the inverter . The inverter is the brain of your solar system. It: Converts DC electricity into usable AC Monitors electricity production in real time Protects your installation against electrical faults Microinverters , installed under each individual panel, allow each module to operate at maximum power. If one panel is shaded or dirty, the others continue to produce normally. What are photovoltaic solar panels made of? Photovoltaic solar panels are mainly composed of silicon cells encapsulated under glass. The choice of materials is key to durability and performance. What are the features of a monocrystalline panel? Single silicon crystal structure High efficiency (from 23% to over 25% for the best models) SunPower panels are made of proprietary encapsulation materials that reduce degradation caused by weather conditions. If you’re a homeowner looking to compare models, you can explore our range of photovoltaic panels . An installer can help assess the best solution for your roof and your needs. What is the efficiency of a solar panel? The efficiency of a solar panel measures the proportion of solar energy converted into electricity. It ranges from 23% to 25% , depending on the technology used. High-efficiency solar panels are engineered with advanced technology to convert more sunlight into usable electricity. In practical terms: A 500 Wp panel (0.5 kWp), properly oriented and installed can produce : in Northern Europe (UK, Sweden, Netherlands between 425 kWh and 500 kWh In Central Europe (France, Germany)between 500 and 700 kWh In Southern Europe (Spain, Greece, Italy) 650-850 kWh per year . As an example, for a home equipped with 6 of our SunPower back-contact panels in Lyon, without shading and a 30° tilt , this represents: 3,250 to 3,940 kWh per year A significant share of a typical household’s electricity consumption Equivalent savings on electricity bills Solar panel performance also depends on: Local sunlight exposure Roof tilt Orientation (ideally facing south, with a 30–35° angle) How does a complete solar panel system work? Here is how solar energy flows through your home, from roof to appliances: Sunlight hits the photovoltaic panels installed on your roof The panels convert this light into direct current The inverter converts it into alternating current The electricity powers your appliances Any excess electricity is either stored in a battery or fed back into the grid Simple, clean, and increasingly efficient: that’s what a photovoltaic solar system looks like today. This applies equally to private homes, commercial buildings, and public infrastructure. SunPower also offers a range of solar solutions designed for businesses and large-scale projects. Self-consumption and selling surplus: what happens to the electricity produced? Self-consumption means directly using the electricity generated by your solar panels. It is the most cost-effective solution: Every kWh consumed is one you don’t buy from the grid Immediate savings on your energy costs When your panels produce more than you consume, the surplus electricity is fed back into the grid. According to the country you live in, you may receive a feed-in tariff - a payment from your energy supplier for each kWh sold. This model, known as self-consumption with surplus sales , helps you maximize the return on your solar project. SunPower energy storage: independence even after sunset Your panels don’t produce electricity at night. That’s why SunPower energy storage makes all the difference. This modular solar battery system allows you to store energy produced during the day for use in the evening, at night, or during cloudy weather. SunPower Home Energy Storage stores excess energy for use anytime, increasing energy independence day and night. Key features: Modular capacity: from 5 kWh up to 20 kWh (stackable units) LFP chemistry (LiFePO₄): safe, stable, cobalt-free technology Depth of discharge: 90% (4.5 kWh usable per 5 kWh installed) Integrated backup power: activates in less than 10 ms in case of outage 4-level protection system: thermal control, adaptive algorithm, IEC62619-certified cells, internal fire suppression system 10-year warranty on product and performance IP65 rating , suitable for demanding environments With an all-in-one app, you can monitor production, consumption, and battery status in real time - one interface, one account, your entire solar energy system under control. Photovoltaic vs. thermal solar panels: what’s the difference? You may have heard of solar thermal panels . These do not produce electricity: they capture heat from solar radiation to heat water or your home. Photovoltaic panels , on the other hand, produce electricity - and are the focus of this guide. There are also hybrid (PVT) panels , which combine both electricity generation and heat recovery. How to install photovoltaic solar panels in UK? Your project must be carried out by a certified professional . This certification may be necessary to access some incentives and will ensure your system is safe. To get started, you can consult SunPower’s network of certified installers , who will support you from design through to commissioning. Take action: your solar journey starts here Now that you understand how photovoltaic panels work, you can see that this technology is not intimidating at all. It is reliable, cost-effective, and accessible - whether you are a homeowner or a business manager . All that’s left is to make the most of the sun that rises every day.

title: PPL Corporation signs Ratepayer Protection Pledge and highlights existing customer protections in Pennsylvania and Kentucky
summary: PPL Corporation today announced it has signed the White House's Ratepayer Protection Pledge, reaffirming the company's long-standing commitment to affordability, reliability and responsible...
body_text: ALLENTOWN, Pa. , July 23, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- PPL Corporation today announced it has signed the White House's Ratepayer Protection Pledge, reaffirming the company's long-standing commitment to affordability, reliability and responsible growth. The pledge, previously signed by many of the nation's largest technology companies, defines voluntary principles to help ensure that data centers appropriately fund energy and infrastructure associated with serving them and that existing customers are protected as demand grows. "The customer-protection principles reflected in the Ratepayer Protection Pledge are consistent with our approach to responsible growth," said Vincent Sorgi, president and chief executive officer of PPL Corporation. "In fact, PPL and its utilities were early movers in establishing new rate classes and regulator-approved, enforceable tariffs designed to protect existing customers and help ensure that large energy users, including data centers, pay their fair share of the costs of infrastructure needed to serve them," said Sorgi. "Ultimately, we believe economic growth and customer protection can go hand in hand, and this pledge reflects that important balance." Advancing customer protections PPL believes many of the principles reflected in the Ratepayer Protection Pledge are already embedded in regulator-approved tariffs and rate structures serving large energy users in its Pennsylvania and Kentucky service territories. In Pennsylvania, PPL Electric Utilities' recently approved LP-6 rate establishes protections ─ including long-term service commitments, minimum billing obligations, revenue protections, up-front payments for directly assignable upgrades, financial security requirements and other measures ─ all designed to ensure costs associated with new demand are paid by customers creating that demand and not shifted to others. Louisville Gas and Electric Company and Kentucky Utilities Company earlier this year implemented similar regulator-approved customer protections through their Extremely High Load Factor (EHLF) tariff. As data centers and other large-load customers connect under these enforceable commitments, they can improve system utilization and potentially lower costs for non-data center customers over time. These approaches demonstrate how economic growth, customer protection and infrastructure investment can advance together through regulator-approved, enforceable mechanisms tailored to the needs of individual states and electric systems. Supporting needed infrastructure Apart from establishing enforceable protections around cost allocation, PPL's utilities are also very focused on protecting grid reliability. Large customer connections are planned carefully, detailed engineering and reliability studies are completed up front, high-demand interconnections are subject to regulatory oversight, and any necessary upgrades are made before service begins, helping to ensure the grid remains safe and reliable for all customers. Additional generation resources will also be needed to support economic growth, strengthen national security, maintain reliability and promote long-term customer affordability. This is why PPL has consistently advocated for policies that encourage investment in new generation resources and energy infrastructure while helping to ensure the costs of serving new demand are appropriately assigned. It's also why PPL created its joint venture with Blackstone Infrastructure ─ to build, own and operate new generation resources needed to serve new data center demand in PJM, particularly in Pennsylvania. The initiative is intended to support reliability, power economic development and help improve the supply-demand balance across the region in an effort to reduce upward pressure on wholesale electricity prices over time. Powering demand that's critical to our nation's economy PPL recognizes that data centers are an essential part of modern life, supporting everything from digital services and business operations to innovation, economic competitiveness and national security. The company's role is to serve this new demand in a way that maintains reliability, protects customers and supports the communities it serves. "At PPL, we are focused on supporting data center growth the right way," said Sorgi. "Reliability comes first. Growth pays for growth. Costs are fair and transparent. Infrastructure is planned with discipline and purpose. And decisions are grounded in clear, coordinated planning. "Ultimately, we believe this growth can deliver significant long-term benefits to the communities we serve. Moving forward, we will continue working with regulators, policymakers and local stakeholders to meet these growing energy needs while keeping energy safe, reliable and affordable for our customers." About PPL PPL Corporation (NYSE: PPL), headquartered in Allentown, Pennsylvania, is a leading U.S. energy company focused on providing electricity and natural gas safely, reliably and affordably to more than 3.6 million customers in the U.S. PPL's high-performing, award-winning utilities are addressing energy challenges head-on by building smarter, more resilient and more dynamic power grids and advancing sustainable energy solutions. For more information, visit www.pplweb.com . Contacts: For news media: Ryan Hill, 610-774-4033 For financial analysts: Andy Ludwig, 610-774-3389 SOURCE PPL Services Corporation

title: Coris MCP: Your merchant risk data, wherever you work
body_text: AI agents are becoming how operational work actually gets done. Not just answering questions, but pulling data, acting on alerts, and completing workflows across the tools your team already uses. The infrastructure making that possible is MCP, Model Context Protocol, the open standard that connects AI tools to the systems your business runs on. Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot all support it. So do Slack, Salesforce, Stripe, HubSpot, and dozens of other platforms teams rely on every day. Most operational workflows have already collapsed into a handful of tools. Sales teams live in Salesforce and Slack. Engineers work in GitHub and their IDE. Risk teams are still the exception: a merchant alert fires, someone opens Coris, cross-references a support ticket, checks a Jira thread, pastes findings into an email. The data exists. The problem is it's spread across different places, and pulling it together is manual every single time. MCP is what finally makes that structural instead of a workaround. The cross-referencing happens in the conversation, not between tabs. Today, Coris joins that ecosystem. Coris MCP connects your merchant risk data and workflows directly to Claude and ChatGPT, so your risk team can ask questions, pull data, and take action without leaving where they work. ‍ What it is Once connected, Claude or ChatGPT has access to your Coris environment: MerchantProfiler signals, CorShield fraud scores, transactions, accounts, and more. Both read and write access, so you can query your portfolio or take action on what you find, without opening Coris separately. A merchant's risk profile isn't static. What looked clean at onboarding can look very different 90 days later. Your AI tool can pull both the current picture and the history in the same conversation, across every signal Coris tracks, without you having to know where to look or which tab to open. It's the same unified view Coris already gives you, now available wherever your team is working. ‍ What you can do with it Get a live read on your portfolio, instantly. Start your day by asking your AI tool what changed overnight. How many alerts came in? Which rules triggered most? Any disputes that need immediate attention? You get a full breakdown in seconds. No dashboard to build, no filters to set. Just ask. Pull a complete merchant picture in one query. Get a flag on a merchant and need the full story fast? Ask your AI tool for everything on that account: name, location, website, transaction rollups, open alerts, notes, account tags. Instead of clicking through tabs in Coris to piece it together, you get the full picture back in one response. From there you can ask follow-up questions, spot patterns across their history, or decide on next steps, all in the same thread. Go from review to action without leaving the conversation. Once you've reviewed a merchant and know what needs to happen, act on it right there. Log a note with your reasoning, update the alert assignment, move the case forward. No tab switch to Coris to record what you decided. The decision and the action stay in the same place. Answer specific questions on demand. Sometimes you need a number fast. "How many high-risk alerts came in this week?" "Which merchants triggered the most rules last month?" "What's the dispute volume trend this quarter?" Ask directly. Your AI tool pulls the answer from your live Coris data. No report builder, no waiting for someone to run a query. ‍ How to get started Coris MCP works with Claude and ChatGPT. To get started in Claude: open Settings → Connectors, add Coris MCP, authenticate through Coris, and start asking. Open Settings → Connectors in Claude. Add the Coris MCP connector using mcp.coris.ai/mcp (or mcp.eu.coris.ai/mcp for EU customers). Log in and grant access through Coris. Start asking. Merchant risk moves fast. Your tools should too. Reach out to your Coris team and we'll get you connected.

summary: Richard Lowenthal, Chief Executive Officer, Transitioning following More than a Decade of Leadership Since Co-Founding the Company Donn Casale, President, Appointed Chief Executive Officer and Director SAN DIEGO, July 07, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- ARS Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
body_text: Releases Details ARS Pharmaceuticals Announces CEO Succession July 7, 2026 PDF Version Richard Lowenthal, Chief Executive Officer, Transitioning following More than a Decade of Leadership Since Co-Founding the Company Donn Casale, President, Appointed Chief Executive Officer and Director SAN DIEGO, July 07, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- ARS Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (Nasdaq: SPRY), a biopharmaceutical company dedicated to empowering at-risk patients and their caregivers to better protect against allergic reactions that could lead to anaphylaxis, today announced a CEO succession, in which co-founder and CEO Richard Lowenthal will no longer serve as an employee and officer of the company effective July 6, 2026. The Board has appointed Donn Casale, currently President, as CEO and Director effective July 7, 2026. “Since co-founding ARS Pharma in 2015, Rich was integral to guiding the company from development to establishing neffy ® as a leading treatment for adults and children with Type 1 allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, and we are grateful for his many contributions,” said Pratik Shah, chairman of the Board of Directors. “As we look ahead, Donn is a seasoned business leader with deep operational and financial acumen, and proven commercial track record, particularly in growing adoption and share in large, consumer-driven markets. We are confident that he has the right background and experience to drive the company through its next phase, growing the neffy franchise and positioning ARS Pharma for both near and long-term value-creation.” Mr. Casale brings more than 25 years of biopharmaceutical business and commercial leadership, with a track record of scaling innovative products in large, patient-driven healthcare markets. Prior to ARS Pharma, he served as Chief Commercial Officer at Dynavax Technologies, where he built the U.S. commercial infrastructure and helped scale the hepatitis B vaccine HEPLISAV-B® from launch to more than $300 million in annualized revenue and over 50% U.S. market share, positioning the company for Sanofi’s $2.2 billion acquisition. Before Dynavax, Mr. Casale held leadership positions in marketing and sales operations at Depomed, supporting the commercialization of GRALISE® and NUCYNTA®. Earlier in his career, he spent 14 years at Merck in progressive roles across sales, marketing, and corporate strategy, contributing to the successful launches of ZOSTAVAX®, GARDASIL®, ROTATEQ®, and PROQUAD®. “I am excited by the opportunity to lead ARS Pharma through its next evolution,” said Mr. Casale. “ neffy is a transformational product for patients, backed by a foundational intranasal technology platform, and I am confident in our ability to grow its impact in the years to come. I’m grateful for the foundation Rich and the Board have built, and I look forward to working alongside our team to increase access, accelerate adoption, and expand the reach of ARS Pharma, delivering on the promise that our treatments can have on patients worldwide.” About neffy ® neffy is a nasal spray used for emergency treatment of allergic reactions including anaphylaxis, in adults and children who weigh 33 lbs. or greater. INDICATION AND IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION FOR neffy (epinephrine nasal spray) INDICATION neffy is indicated for emergency treatment of type I allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, in adult and pediatric patients who weigh 33 lbs. or greater. IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION neffy contains epinephrine, a medicine used to treat allergic emergencies (anaphylaxis). Anaphylaxis can be life-threatening, can happen in minutes, and can be caused by stinging and biting insects, allergy injections, foods, medicines, exercise, or other unknown causes. Always carry two neffy nasal sprays with you because you may not know when anaphylaxis may happen and because you may need a second dose of neffy if symptoms continue or come back. Each neffy contains a single dose of epinephrine. neffy is for use in the nose only. Use neffy right away, as soon as you notice symptoms of an allergic reaction. If symptoms continue or get worse after the first dose of neffy , a second dose is needed. If needed, administer a second dose using a new neffy in the same nostril starting 5 minutes after the first dose. Get emergency medical help for further treatment of the allergic emergency (anaphylaxis), if needed after using neffy . Tell your healthcare provider if you have underlying structural or anatomical nasal conditions, about all the medicines you take, and about all your medical conditions, especially if you have heart problems, kidney problems, low potassium in your blood, Parkinson's disease, thyroid problems, high blood pressure, diabetes, are pregnant or plan to become pregnant, or plan to breastfeed. Tell your healthcare provider if you take or use other nasal sprays or water pills (diuretics) or if you take medicines to treat depression, abnormal heart beats, Parkinson's disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, medicines used in labor, and medicines to treat allergies. neffy and other medications may affect each other, causing side effects. neffy may affect the way other medicines work, and other medicines may affect how neffy works. neffy may cause serious side effects. If you have certain medical conditions or take certain medicines, your condition may get worse, or you may have more or longer lasting side effects when you use neffy . Common side effects of neffy include: nasal discomfort, headache, throat irritation, chest and nasal congestion, feeling overly excited, nervous or anxious, nose bleed, nose pain, sneezing, runny nose, dry nose or throat, tingling sensation, including in the nose, feeling tired, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. Tell your healthcare provider if you have any side effects that bother you or that do not go away after using neffy . These are not all of the possible side effects of neffy . Call your healthcare provider for medical advice about side effects. To report side effects, contact ARS Pharmaceuticals Operations, Inc. at 1-877-MY-NEFFY (877-696-3339) or the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088 or www.fda.gov/medwatch . Please see the full Prescribing Information and Patient Information for neffy . About Type I Allergic Reactions Including Anaphylaxis Type I allergic reactions are serious and potentially life-threatening events that can occur within minutes of exposure to an allergen and require immediate treatment with epinephrine, the only FDA-approved medication for these reactions. While epinephrine auto-injectors have been shown to be highly effective, there are well published limitations that result in many patients and caregivers delaying or not administering treatment in an emergency situation. These limitations include fear of the needle, lack of portability, needle-related safety concerns, lack of reliability, and complexity of the devices. There are approximately 40 million people in the United States who experience Type I allergic reactions. Of this group, over the last three years, approximately 20 million people have been diagnosed and treated for severe Type I allergic reactions that may lead to anaphylaxis, but (in 2023, for example) only 3.2 million filled their active epinephrine auto-injector prescription, and of those, only half consistently carry their prescribed auto-injector. Even if patients or caregivers carry an auto-injector, more than half either delay or do not administer the device when needed in an emergency. About ARS Pharmaceuticals, Inc. ARS Pharma is a biopharmaceutical company dedicated to empowering at-risk patients and their caregivers to better protect patients against allergic reactions that could lead to anaphylaxis. The Company is commercializing neffy ® (trade name EUR neffy ® in the EU and UK and 优敏速® in China), an epinephrine nasal spray indicated in the U.S. for emergency treatment of Type I allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, in adult patients and pediatric patients who weigh 33 lbs. or greater, and in the EU for emergency treatment of allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) due to insect stings or bites, foods, medicinal products, and other allergens as well as idiopathic or exercise induced anaphylaxis in adults and children who weigh 15 kg or greater. title: After Hours Trading: How It Works, Risks, and the Brokers (2026 Guide)
summary: Learn how after hours trading works, including extended-hours market sessions, risks, rules, and the brokers for US investors in 2026. Compare platforms like Webull and discover how to trade stocks after market close.
body_text: After hours trading lets US investors buy and sell stocks after the regular market closes at 4:00 p.m. ET. Once reserved for institutions, the after hours stock market is now accessible to everyday traders through modern brokerage platforms. Whether you're reacting to an earnings report or breaking news, understanding how these extended-hours sessions work — and their unique risks — can help you trade smarter. This guide breaks down the mechanics, benefits, risks, and the top platforms available today. Table of Contents Part 1: What Is After Hours Trading? Understanding the After Hours Stock Market Part 2: How After Hours Market Trading Works: Hours, Risks, and Rules Part 3: Brokers for After Hours Share Trading in the US (2026) FAQs The Bottom Line Part 1: What Is After Hours Trading? Understanding the After Hours Stock Market After hours trading is the buying and selling of stocks and ETFs through electronic markets after the regular US session closes at 4:00 p.m. ET, typically running until 8:00 p.m. ET. Together with the pre-market session, it forms what traders call "extended-hours" trading. Historically, only banks and hedge funds could participate in after hours market trading. Today, ECNs and commission-free brokerage apps have opened the after hours stock exchange to retail investors, letting them respond to news the moment it breaks instead of waiting for the next opening bell. Why traders use the after hours session React to earnings: Most US companies report earnings after 4:00 p.m. ET. After hours share trading lets you respond immediately. Trade breaking news: Fed announcements, mergers, and guidance updates often land outside regular hours. Track after market movers: Big overnight gainers and losers frequently set the tone for the next day's open. Fit your schedule: Working professionals can manage positions in the evening. Extended-hours sessions at a glance Session Typical Hours (ET) Who Trades Pre-market 4:00 a.m. – 9:30 a.m. Early reactors, news traders Regular market 9:30 a.m. – 4:00 p.m. All participants After hours 4:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m. Earnings and news traders Exact windows vary by broker; some offer overnight sessions that extend the after hours stock market nearly around the clock on trading days. Part 2: How After Hours Market Trading Works: Hours, Risks, and Rules During regular hours, orders route to major exchanges with deep liquidity. In the after hours market, orders are matched through ECNs. This structural difference drives every benefit and every risk below. 3.1 How to place an after hours trade (step by step) Open an eligible brokerage account that supports extended-hours trading. Enable extended-hours trading in your order settings or account preferences. Select the stock and review its after hours quote and volume. Choose a limit order — most brokers require limit orders after hours to protect you from bad fills. Set your session (pre-market, after hours, or overnight, where available). Review and submit , then monitor the order, since it may only fill partially or not at all. After hours trading generally runs from 4:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET , immediately after the regular US stock market closes. Some brokers extend stock trading after hours market access into overnight sessions. 3.2 The main risks of after hours trading The after hours stock exchange behaves differently from the regular session in ways that can catch traders off guard. With most institutional desks offline and far fewer participants active, prices can move faster and less predictably on lighter volume, and the quotes you see may not reflect true, executable demand. That combination makes extended-hours trading higher-risk than a typical daytime trade, so it pays to understand what you're stepping into. Know these risks before you place an order in the after hours market: Lower liquidity: Fewer buyers and sellers make it harder to enter or exit at your target price. Wider bid-ask spreads: Thin volume can push the gap between buy and sell prices much wider. Higher volatility: Small orders can move prices sharply, especially around earnings. Limited order types: Many brokers only allow limit orders during extended hours. Price gaps: An after hours price may differ significantly from the next day's open. 3.3 Regulation, safety, and investor protection Trustworthy after hours share trading depends on where you trade. In the US, reputable brokers are: FINRA-regulated members, subject to conduct and reporting rules. SEC-registered , operating under federal securities law. SIPC members , protecting securities up to $500,000 (including a $250,000 limit for cash) if the brokerage fails. SIPC does not protect against market losses. Before trading the after hours market, confirm your broker's regulatory status on FINRA BrokerCheck and review its risk disclosures. Platform safety features such as two-factor authentication, encryption, and account-activity alerts add another layer of protection. Webull — A Standout for After Hours and Overnight Trading Webull is the comprehensive platform for after hours trading in our ranking, pairing some of the longest extended-hours access available to retail traders with professional-grade tools at $0 commission. Securities are offered by Webull Financial LLC, an SEC-registered broker-dealer and a member of FINRA, SIPC, NYSE, NASDAQ, and Cboe EDGX. Why Webull leads for extended-hours traders Webull is built for active traders who want to treat the after hours stock market seriously, not casually. Between pre-market, after hours, and a dedicated overnight session, Webull effectively offers trading 24 hours a day, 5 days a week on select securities — a level of after hours market access most mainstream brokers don't match at zero commission. SIPC member. 4. E*TRADE (Morgan Stanley) Reliable extended-hours sessions and a polished platform. Good for traders who value a balance of tools and support. SIPC member. 5. Robinhood Simple, mobile-first after hours share trading with an extended overnight session. Best for casual traders who prioritize ease of use over advanced tooling. SIPC member. FAQs 1. What is after hours trading in simple terms? After hours trading is buying and selling stocks through electronic networks after the regular US market closes at 4:00 p.m. ET, usually until 8:00 p.m. ET. It lets investors react to news and earnings outside standard hours. 2. Is after hours trading a good idea for beginners? It can be risky for beginners because the after hours market has lower liquidity, wider spreads, and higher volatility. New traders should start with limit orders, small positions, and ideally practice with paper trading first. 3. Can you make money trading after hours? Yes, traders can profit by reacting quickly to earnings and after market movers, but the same volatility that creates opportunity also increases the risk of losses and poor fills. 4. What time does after hours trading end? Standard after hours trading ends at 8:00 p.m. ET. Some brokers, such as Webull, offer overnight sessions that extend stock trading after hours market access well beyond that window. 5. Why is the after hours price different from the closing price? Because the after hours stock exchange has fewer participants, even modest orders can move prices, causing after hours quotes to differ from both the 4:00 p.m. close and the next day's open. 6. Do all brokers offer after hours share trading? No. Availability, session length, and order-type rules vary by broker, so confirm extended-hours support and any limit-order requirements before you trade. The Bottom Line After hours trading gives US investors the flexibility to act on news and earnings the moment they break — but thin liquidity and volatility demand discipline and limit orders. If you want long extended-hours access, real-time data, and pro-grade tools at $0 commission, Webull is our top pick. Compare your options, confirm the protections, and trade the plan. title: 9 Options Strategies You Can Backtest With AI
summary: If you want to options strategies backtest with AI, start with structures where rules, risk, and expiration behavior can be defined clearly. AI can…
body_text: If you want to options strategies backtest with AI , start with structures where rules, risk, and expiration behavior can be defined clearly. AI can help convert trade ideas into testable logic, compare outcomes across regimes, and expose whether a setup depends on unrealistic timing, liquidity, or volatility assumptions. Options are harder to backtest than stocks because every trade has more moving parts: strike, expiry, implied volatility, Greeks, bid-ask spread, assignment risk, and event timing. The best options strategy backtesting workflows make those assumptions explicit before a trader commits capital. ​ Quick Comparison: Options Strategies to Backtest With AI Strategy Best for testing Main risk to inspect Covered calls Income against stock holdings Capped upside Cash-secured puts Entry discipline and premium collection Downside stock exposure Long calls Directional upside Time decay Long puts Downside protection or bearish trades Premium loss Vertical spreads Defined-risk directional views Poor reward-to-risk Iron condors Range-bound markets Volatility expansion Straddles Event volatility Expensive premium Calendars Term-structure views Complex volatility shifts Earnings strategies Event-driven setups Gap and IV crush risk ​ 1. Covered Calls Covered calls are one of the cleanest strategies to test because the structure is simple: own shares, sell calls, collect premium, and accept capped upside. AI can help test different call deltas, expirations, rolling rules, and market regimes. For example, a trader may compare weekly covered calls versus 30- to 45-day expirations, or test whether selling calls after sharp rallies improves results. The key variables are: Call delta or moneyness Days to expiration Roll or close rules Underlying selection Dividend and earnings filters A useful AI options trading platform should show whether the premium meaningfully improves risk-adjusted returns or simply gives up too much upside during strong trends. ​ 2. Cash-Secured Puts Cash-secured puts are often described as a way to get paid while waiting to buy a stock. That description is incomplete. The strategy is still long downside risk. Backtesting helps traders see whether the put premium compensates for that risk. AI can compare selling puts at different deltas, avoiding earnings weeks, requiring valuation filters, or only selling after volatility spikes. Important questions include: How often would assignment occur? What happens during market selloffs? Does implied volatility justify the premium? Is the strategy better than simply buying the stock? An AI strategy backtest should separate income from risk transfer. Premium is not free money; it is compensation for taking defined exposure. ​ 3. Long Calls Long calls are simple to understand but difficult to trade well. The direction can be right while the option still loses money because timing, implied volatility, or strike selection was poor. AI can help test when long calls have historically worked best: breakouts, post-earnings momentum, analyst upgrades, high relative strength, or broad market risk-on conditions. Backtest variations should include: In-the-money versus out-of-the-money calls Short-dated versus longer-dated expirations Profit-taking and stop-loss rules Filters for spread width and liquidity Avoiding periods of elevated implied volatility The goal is to determine whether leverage improves the setup or simply magnifies decay. ​ 4. Long Puts Long puts can be used for bearish trades or portfolio protection. In both cases, backtesting matters because puts are often expensive when fear is already visible. AI can test whether puts work better after volatility compression, trend breakdowns, weak breadth, earnings risk, or macro stress signals. It can also compare outright puts with put spreads to see whether defined upside is worth the lower premium. Useful metrics include hit rate, average loss, payoff skew, drawdown protection, and cost of carry. A good backtest should also show how often the hedge expired worthless. For hedging, the question is not whether every put makes money. The question is whether the strategy reduces unacceptable portfolio risk at a reasonable cost. ​ 5. Vertical Spreads Vertical spreads are useful because they define risk and reward in advance. Traders can test bull call spreads, bear put spreads, bear call spreads, and bull put spreads using different strikes and expirations. AI can help compare spread width, entry timing, delta selection, and exits based on profit targets or time remaining. This is where options backtesting software becomes valuable: small changes in strike choice can materially change expectancy. Backtest these assumptions: Debit versus credit structure Short-leg delta Days to expiration Exit at 50%, 75%, or expiration Liquidity and bid-ask spread filters Vertical spreads are often better than outright options when the trader wants a defined thesis rather than unlimited optionality. ​ 6. Iron Condors Iron condors are designed for range-bound markets. They collect premium by selling an out-of-the-money call spread and put spread, but they can suffer when volatility expands or price trends aggressively. AI can test which environments are most favorable: falling realized volatility, post-event volatility crush, low trend strength, or mean-reverting index behavior. Key variables include wing width, short-delta selection, days to expiration, stop-loss rules, and whether to close early after collecting a set percentage of max profit. Backtesting should focus less on win rate and more on loss size. Many condor strategies look attractive until a few large losses erase months of premium. ​ 7. Long Straddles and Strangles Long straddles and strangles are volatility trades. The trader is not just betting on direction; they are betting that realized movement will exceed the premium paid. AI can test these strategies around earnings, product announcements, macro releases, litigation events, or unusually compressed volatility. It can also compare at-the-money straddles with wider strangles. The most important backtest questions are: Was implied volatility already too high? How large was the realized move? Did the move happen quickly enough? Were spreads wide around the event? Did exits improve results versus holding to expiration? These strategies can produce dramatic winners, but the base rate matters. AI helps separate memorable trades from repeatable setups. ​ 8. Calendar Spreads Calendar spreads use options with different expirations, usually to express a view on time decay and volatility term structure. They are more nuanced than simple directional trades. AI can test whether calendars work better before earnings, after volatility spikes, during quiet index periods, or when short-term implied volatility differs meaningfully from longer-term implied volatility. The backtest should include changes in implied volatility, not just price movement. Calendar spreads can behave unexpectedly when both the underlying and volatility surface move at the same time. For advanced traders, this is where an AI options trading platform should provide transparency around Greeks, term structure, and exit assumptions. ​ 9. Earnings Options Strategies Earnings are ideal for AI-assisted testing because the event timing is clear and the option market often prices in a large move. Traders can test long premium, short premium, spreads, or post-earnings continuation trades. Backtesting should compare implied move versus realized move, pre-event IV behavior, post-event IV crush, gap direction, liquidity, and whether waiting until after the report improves risk-adjusted results. Potential tests include: Buying straddles before earnings Selling iron condors after IV spikes Trading post-earnings drift with calls or puts Using spreads instead of outright options Avoiding names with poor liquidity For traders moving from research to execution, platforms like Scalar Field can help convert a verified earnings-options hypothesis into an agent that monitors calendars, liquidity, risk limits, and broker-connected deployment rules. ​ How to Evaluate Options Backtesting Software Options backtests are only as good as their assumptions. Before trusting results, confirm that the tool handles real contracts rather than synthetic shortcuts. Look for: Historical option chains Bid, ask, and mid-price handling Implied volatility and Greeks Expiration and strike selection rules Liquidity and open interest filters Earnings and event calendars Transaction cost assumptions Assignment and exercise logic where relevant Clear logs of every simulated trade If a platform hides contract selection, ignores spreads, or assumes fills at unrealistic prices, the output will be misleading. ​ Final Thoughts There are many options strategies backtest with AI , but the best candidates are the ones with clear rules and measurable risks. Covered calls, cash-secured puts, long calls, long puts, vertical spreads, iron condors, straddles, calendars, and earnings trades all benefit from structured testing. AI does not make options risk disappear. It helps traders define the trade, test the assumptions, compare variations, and avoid deploying strategies that only looked good because the backtest was too generous.
